Chapter 2: The Roots of East Asian and American Values
Every culture has its own story about what really matters. These stories—they’re passed down through families, taught in classrooms, and echoed by leaders. They quietly shape how people see themselves and where they fit in this big, complicated world.
So, if you’ve ever wondered why China and the United States act so differently, it helps to look at where their core values come from.
In East Asia, Confucius casts a long shadow—even after thousands of years. His teachings aren’t just about rules or laws; they’re about relationships. At the heart of Confucian thought is this idea: society works best when everyone understands their role and treats others with respect.
Picture the family as the blueprint for all relationships—parents guide children, rulers guide citizens, and everyone has duties to each other.
This isn’t just about how families work; it influences how governments are run too. Leaders are expected to act like wise parents, looking out for the group and putting the community’s needs above their own. People grow up learning to value harmony, avoid open conflict, and search for consensus. There’s a deep belief that stability is precious, and real change should come slowly—and always with the entire community in mind.
Here’s a story that brings this to life. Imagine a young professional in Beijing who’s offered a dream job in another city—but her parents are aging and need her nearby. Her friends encourage her to follow her ambitions, but she feels a powerful pull to stay close to home. In the end, she chooses family over career—not because she isn’t driven, but because, for her, personal success is tied to the well-being of those she loves. Duty and happiness? For her, they’re not opposites. They’re deeply connected.
Meanwhile, in the United States, the founding story is all about breaking free from old limits. Early settlers, many escaping persecution, built a society that prizes individual rights and self-reliance. The Declaration of Independence—with its famous promise of “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness”—set the tone for everything that followed.
You can see this spirit every day. Kids are encouraged to speak their minds, ask questions, and dream as big as they can. There’s a real sense that, if you work hard enough, you can make it—no matter where you start. The government’s job? To protect freedom, not to act as a wise parent. When challenges come up, Americans are quick to look for new solutions, even if it means questioning old traditions.
Picture a small-town entrepreneur, frustrated by endless red tape, starting a business out of her garage. Even when she stumbles, she keeps going—believing that her ideas matter. Her story gets celebrated as proof that anyone can succeed, no matter their background. For her, freedom and responsibility go hand in hand.
Now, these two sets of values—harmony and duty on one side, freedom and innovation on the other—they don’t have to be in conflict. In fact, they can actually complement one another. The American drive for progress can learn from East Asia’s focus on stability and long-term thinking. And the Confucian respect for relationships? It can help balance out the extremes of individualism.
But here’s something to watch out for: it’s easy to get stuck seeing only the differences. When misunderstandings happen, each side might see the other as stubborn or naive. The real challenge is to spot the strengths in both traditions—and find ways to bring them together.
As the world faces problems that no country can solve alone, this kind of cross-cultural understanding becomes more important than ever. The stories we tell ourselves about what matters most—they’re not just shaping our own futures, but the future of the whole planet.
